newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader to press Russia over independence.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader to press Russia over independence.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov flew to Moscow on Monday to seek Russian President Boris Yeltsin's formal recognition of his breakaway region's effective independence, Interfax news agency said.
"The main aim of the visit is to communicate Chechnya's position on relations with Russia to the Russian president," Interfax quoted Maskhadov as saying before leaving Grozny, the Chechen capital.

"These relations should be equal, based on a full-scale inter-state treaty which would envisage mutual recognition, establishing embassies and non-interference in each other's internal affairs," Maskhadov added.

Russian officials have made clear that they are not willing even to discuss Chechnya's claims to full independence which they see as a breach of a peace deal signed a year ago August after 20 months of war in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
Under the peace deal, Russia pulled its forces out of the rebel region and the separatist leaders agreed to delay a decision on Chechnya's future political status until 2001.
The rebel leaders say their region is independent and they view the delay simply as a breathing space for Moscow to find a face-saving way of letting Chechnya formally secede.
The Chechen first deputy prime minister, Movladi Udugov, also said on Sunday that Chechen was demanding that Moscow pay for the damage wrought by its troops during the fighting.

"Russia is obliged by all moral norms to restore what it destroyed," he said. Chechnya puts the total cost of restoring its economy and infrastructure at a staggering $260 billion -- more than half Russia's entire annual national income.
Moscow views Chechnya as part of the Russian federation and hopes that in four years it will find a compromise with Grozny which would keep the region from seceding.
Russian officials have said that Yeltsin is planning to discuss with Maskhadov Moscow's economic assistance to Chechnya.

He will also urge Maskhadov to free Russians and a number of foreigners still being held in Chechnya and make efforts to clamp down on banditry, which has flourished in the southern province for years.
Udugov said on Sunday that two journalists from a private Russian television company, seized on June 11, had been freed on the eve of the talks.
Three jounalists from the NTV commercial channel, seized more than three months ago, are still in captivity somewhere in Chechnya.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those currently missing in Chechnya.
Russian Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin, the main Kremlin negotiator with Chechnya, has said the number of people still missing, including captives taken during the war, totals 1,407.
